text:
Ontario Superior Court of Justice

Toiber v.
Toiber

Date:
2005-10-26

Roselyn Zisman for Applicant, Father

Lawrence Goldapple for Respondent, Mother

Docket: 05-FA-13499FIS

Hoilett J. :

[
1
]

This is an application by the father, brought
pursuant to Section 15 of the Convention of the Civil Aspects of International
Child Abduction (the "Hague Convention"), for a declaration that
Liliya
1
* Toiber, born May 15, 1992, and Alis*
Toiber, born May 25, 1997, are being wrongfully retained, and for an order that
the two children be returned, forthwith, to their habitual residence, namely,
Israel.

[
2
]

The essential facts are not seriously in
dispute. The parties were married in Ukraine on December 26, 1990 and the two
children in dispute are the product of that marriage. Liliya was born in
Ukraine and Alis was born in Israel, to which the couple had immigrated in
1994.

[
3
]

The couple were divorced on September 11, 2003;
the terms of which divorce granted custody of the children to the mother with
visitation rights to the father. That right of visitation was, at all material
times, being exercised by the father.

[
4
]

Upon application by the father, the Israeli
court granted leave for the mother to take the children out of the jurisdiction
of the Israeli court, conditioned upon the children being returned to Israel by
September 1, 2004. That order granting leave to remove the children was
obtained sometime in July 2004 and it was with the father's consent. The common
understanding was that the children were being taken to Czechoslovakia to visit
the mother's sister. Some issue was raised concerning whether the children were
ever taken to Czechoslovakia, and, if so, for how long; what is not in issue is
the fact that they were taken to Canada.

[
5
]

That "detour" to Canada by the mother
was without the father's knowledge or consent. The father learnt sometime in
September 2004 that the mother and children were in Canada, but, as of the date
of this hearing, he has never been informed of their specific whereabouts. All
indications are that that secrecy is deliberate. This application was launched
by the father in December 2004, well within the twelve-month period allowed for
the launching of such an application.

[
6
]

The mother, since her arrival in Canada, has
launched a refugee claim on her own behalf and on behalf of the two children.
That application, as averred to by the mother in an affidavit sworn/affirmed
August 22, 2005, has met the threshold requirement for such applications.

[
7
]

Before turning to a review of some of the claims
made by the mother, reference might usefully be made to relevant provisions of
the Hague Convention, including its "preamble", which, the
authorities say, is relevant to its proper interpretation. (ref.
Thomson v.
Thomson
(1994),
1994 CanLII 26 (SCC)
, 6 R.F.L. (4th) 290 (S.C.C.), at 302).

[Preamble]

The States signatory to the present
Convention.

Firmly convinced that the interests of
children are of paramount importance…

Desiring to protect children
internationally from the harmful effects of their wrongful removal or retention
and to establish procedures to ensure their prompt return to the State of their
habitual residence, as well as to secure protection for rights of access,

Have resolved to conclude a Convention to
this effect, and have agreed upon the following provisions:

Article 1

The objects of the present Convention are:

(a) to secure the prompt return of children wrongfully removed to or
retained in any Contracting State; and

(b) to ensure that rights of custody and of access under the law of
one Contracting State are effectively respected in the other Contracting
States.

Article 3

The removal or the retention of a child is
to be considered wrongful where:

(a) it is in breach of rights of custody attributed to a person, an
institution or any other body, either jointly or alone, under the law of the
State in which the child was habitually resident immediately before the removal
or retention; and

(b) at the time of removal or retention those rights were actually
exercised, either jointly or alone, or would have been so exercised but for the
removal or retention.

The rights of custody mentioned in
sub-paragraph (a) above, may arise in particular by operation of law or by
reason of a judicial or administrative decision, or by reason of an agreement
having legal effect under the law of that State.

Article 5

For the purposes of this Convention:

(a) "rights of custody" shall include rights relating to
the care of the person of the child and, in particular, the right to determine
the child's place of residence;

(b) "rights of access" shall include the right to take a
child for a limited period of time to a place other than the child's habitual
residence.

Article 11

The judicial or administrative authorities
of Contracting States shall act expeditiously in proceedings for the return of
children.

…

Article 13

Notwithstanding the provisions of the
preceding Article, the judicial or administrative authority of the requested
State is not bound to order the return of the child if the person, institution
or other body which opposes its return establishes that:

(a) …

(b) there is a grave risk that his or her return would expose the
child to physical or psychological harm or otherwise place the child in an intolerable
situation.

The judicial or administrative authority
may also refuse to order the return of the child if it finds that the child
objects to being returned and has attained an age and a degree of maturity at
which it is appropriate to take account of its views.

In considering the circumstances referred
to in this Article, the judicial and , administrative authorities shall take
into account the information relating to the social background of the child
provided by the Central Authority or other competent authority of the child's
habitual residence

Article 16

After receiving notice of a wrongful
removal of retention of a child in the sense of Article 3, the judicial or
administrative authorities of the contracting State to which the child has been
removed or in which it has been retained shall not determine the merits of the
rights of custody until it has been determined that the child is not to be
returned under the Convention …

[
8
]

The
Convention
has been incorporated by
reference to form a part of the Ontario law relating to child welfare, as
appears in Section 46 of the
Children Law Reform Act,
R.S.O. 1990, chap.
C.12
:

46.-(1)  In this section "convention" means the Convention
on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction, set out in the Schedule
to this section. ("convention")

(2)         On, from and after the 1
st
day of December,
1983, except as provided in subsection 3, [not here relevant] the convention is
in force in Ontario and the provisions thereof are law in Ontario.

[
9
]

Ms. Tobier predicates her opposition to the
application on Article 13 of the
Convention, supra.
The evidence on
which she relies is set out in her affidavit, dated August 22, 2005, earlier
referred to. Ms. Tobier, seventeen years old at the time of her marriage,
asserts to the following, among other things: She was born in Odessa, Ukraine
on September 18, 1973 but is currently a citizen of Israel only. Her husband is
Jewish and she, who is not, has been effectively disowned by his family and
"hated by them from the first day of our engagement". Her husband's
parents, when they were repatriated to Israel in 1994, forced him to follow
them and she had no choice in the matter. Ms. Toiber claims that her
parents-in-law lured her husband to Israel because they thought it would be
easier for him to obtain a divorce there "and to persuade him to marry a
Jewish girl". Ms. Tobier asserts that her in-laws were ultimately
successful because her husband began to hate her. And, in paragraph 6 of her
affidavit:

6. After my divorce my husband would
persecute me. He would telephone me with threats to come by my house and force
sex on me any time he wished to do so. He also called me vile names. As he had
a right to visit our daughter, he used that visit to try to sexually assault
me. Sometimes he was successful in the sexual assault without my consent. Twice
I reported these incidents to the police and my divorce lawyer. The police just
laughed at me and dismissed my complaints outright and my lawyer simply stated
that these types of problems were hard to resolve if one of the spouses was
non-Jewish.

7. At that time my husband began to
threaten to take away our daughters. He said our daughters had to be with a
Jewish mother and not with a "goim" (non-Jewish) mother. This was ironic since he was not a good father
himself. Our daughters told me that during their visits to his house they saw
drunken people (including my husband) and that their father had not paid
attention to them forcing them to play alone for hours. The Respondent would
also race cars with the children in it while drunk. I could not do anything to
change that situation as the divorce order favoured him because he was Jewish
and I was not.

8. On two occasions I had to escape from my
ex-husband and seek protection from my friends who live in different places in
Israel. However, each time my husband was able to discover my shelter and come
for me. He would say that I was his slave forever. On one occasion I was forced
to seek protection at a women's shelter.

9. My daughters both experienced bad
treatment in Israel as well. Other children would call them names as
"goim" or "dirty Russians". Many times they would return
home from school in tears. I tried to complain to the administration of their
school, but administration turned a blind eye to my problems by telling me that
nothing wrong was happening.

10. My life in Israel became unbearable for
me and my daughters. Accordingly, I obtained permission to visit my sister in
the Czech Republic which I did. I bought a ticket and left Israel for the Czech
Republic.

11. I then decided that neither my children
nor I could safely return to Israel and I bought a ticket to Canada where I
learned that I might seek refugee status for myself and my children.

[
10
]

Ms. Toiber averred, further, that the children
are enrolled in school here and are settled and doing well. And, further, that
she believes that "there" is a grave risk that the children's return
to Israel would expose the children to both physical and psychological harm or
otherwise place the children in an intolerable situation. In paragraph 17, she
avers that she believes that both of the children "object to being
returned".

[
11
]

Common sense, if nothing else, suggests caution
I making findings of credibility based on affidavits, particularly there has
been no cross-examination on those affidavits. That having been said, the
affidavit sworn by Ms. Toiber given, the nature of its claims, invites the
following comments. Except for the fact that she was awarded custody of the
children, she has rather been ill done by the Israeli society; assuming her
claims to be true. What, in my view, is remarkable is the absence of any
corroboration for any of Ms. Toiber's assertions. At a
very minimum, one would have expected some corroboration, sworn or otherwise,
from someone at the women's shelter attended by Ms. Toiber. Similarly, one
might reasonably have expected some form of corroboration from the friends
whose shelter she sought; as indeed would be the expectation from her divorce
lawyer to whom she claimed to have complained. Equally significant, in my view,
is the absence of any record of the children's performance in school in Israel
which renders meaningless a record of their performance at school in Canada;
given that there is no basis for a comparison. Taking Ms. Toiber's affidavit at face value, one might reasonably have expected two
traumatized children and appropriate professional intervention. I expressly
raised that question during the hearing and it is common ground that there has
been no such intervention, neither here nor in Israel.

[
12
]

Concerning Ms. Toiber's reliance
on exceptions contemplated by
Article 13,
she relies as well on a
hand-printed note of her daughter, "Liliya", which forms
Exhibit
"A"
to Mrs. Toiber's affidavit sworn September 14, 2005. In order
to preserve the integrity of the sentiments expressed by Liliya, I have
reproduced following her hand-printed note:

September 12, 2005

TO       Rozelin Zisman

Igor Toiber's

Lawyer

My name is Lilia Toiber.

My mom's name is Olga Toiber.

My little sister's name is Alise
Toiber.

I want you to know that my father

never cared about me or my sister (Alise).

He was always mean to me,

He always yelled at me,

He never wanted to hear what is in

my heart.

He always said that I'm a little girl and

I don't understand anything.

I hate this person,

and I never want to see him, hear him or

Hear about him.

I don't want from him anything.

I don't want him to come near me again.

I want him to leave my mom me and

My sister, alone.

I'd rather to live without father instead

of having father like he is.

Lilia Toiber

(
Ex. A.
to Mrs. Toiber's

September 14, 2005 affidavit)

[
13
]

The following other facts bear on the issues to
be decided.

[
14
]

Mr. Toiber, in paragraph 18 of his affidavit,
sworn May 31, 2005, relies on the following assurance:

18. The Central Authority of the State of
Israel has confirmed that pursuant to Sections 14 and 15 of Israel's Capacity
and Guardianship Law (1962), parents are the joint guardians of their children
and the right of guardianship also includes the right to determine the children's
place of residence…

[
15
]

Forming a part of the STATE OF ISRAEL REQUEST
FOR RETURN OF ABDUCTED CHILDREN, and being
Ex.
"
A
"

to
Mr. Toiber's affidavit, is the text of Section 14 and
15, cited from Vol. 16, "LAWS OF THE STATE OF ISRAEL".

CAPACITY
AND GUARDIANSHIP LAW,

5722 - 1962

CHAPTER
TWO; PARENTS AND MINOR CHILDREN

Status of parents:                                                  14.
Parents shall be the natural guardians of their children.

Functions of parents:                                             15.
The guardianship of the parents shall include the duty and the right to take
care of the needs of the minor, including his education, studies, vocational
and occupational training and work, and to preserve, manage and develop his
property; it shall also include the right to the custody of the minor, to
determine his place of residence and the authority to act on his behalf.

(APPLICANT'S RECORD, Part and Volume: Part II, Volume 1, Tab 3,
between pages 28 and 29)

[
16
]

The Israeli Court's decision granting the
couples divorce, and dated 11/09/2003, incorporates a contract between the
parties. The "Court Decision" signifies that "the partners made
the contract of their free will and understanding its meaning and
results". Made Appendix I to the Court Decision, the "CONTRACT OF
PROPERTY RELATIONS, ALIMONIES AND DIVORCE" provides among other things:

3. Children Maintenance

(a) The Father agrees that the children will stay in disposal of
their mother and on her maintenance, with subjection to the Mother of taking of
the children and meetings, and all as it is said in this Contract.

(b) The mother commits herself to care for all the needs and
proverties (sic) of the children up to the age 18, as according to commitments
of the Mother, as it is said in this contract.

(c) The Father will have a right to take the children for meeting in
a way coordinated between the parties and with taking into account the
possibilities of the children and the Wife, but not less as every second
Saturday, from Friday when the children finish their studies at school and
until 20:00 on Saturday night and also one time a week on Wednesday from 16:00
until 20:00.

(d) The parties commit themselves and declare that they will care
for education of the children by the way of respect and appreciation towards
the Father and the Mother, and will prevent animosity (sic), and/or disregard
and/or slander and/or reduction and harm in recpect (sic) of the Father and/or
of the Mother or of the families of the Father and the Mother and/or the
partners of the Father and/or the Mother, if they will marry and/or will Jive
with other partner.

(e) There is agreed that the partners will discover one to another
any vital information concerning the children and will meet the other partner
if he will ask for information about the children.

The partners
commit themselves to consult one with another in any matter in respect of
education of the children, their studies and health, and also about
celebrations of birthdays, school year completion party etc.

(f) The Husband will have a right to take the children for the
period of holidays and school vacations.

(g) The partners commit themselves not to take the children abroad,
only on agreement of both partners before hand and in a written form.

(ref.
Applicant's Record, Part II, Volume 1, Tab 3, pp. 20-21)

[
17
]

It was pursuant to sub-paragraph (g), cited
above, that a request was made to the Court for leave to take the children
abroad; as appear from the following:

REQUEST
TO CANCEL STOP-ORDER

In re Igor Toiber

I, Igor Toiber…hereby request this
Honorable Court to cancel the stop-order applicable to my children, Liliya
Toiber, … and Alis Toiber, … I request to permit my children to travel abroad
for a short period, until the first of September (01/09/04). My request is
intended to further my children's right to visit their relatives abroad during
the school vacation. I am obliged to point out that my present request does not
contradict and does not cancel my prior request submitted on 02/06/04, in which
I express opposition to my children's leaving to go abroad without my consent
for an extended period.

With thanks in advance

Igor Toiber (signed)

DECISION
(handwritten)

1. On the basis of the parties' agreement, I hereby order the
canceling of the stop-order against the minors Liliya and Alis Toiber.

2. It is incumbent upon the mother to return the minors to Israel no
later than the date 1.9.04.

[signed and
stamped Jacob Cohen, Judge, Family Court; 15-07-2004; Kefar Suba(1)]

(ref.
Applicant's Record, Vol. 1, Part II, Tab 3, page 30)

[
18
]

It having been conceded that Israel is "the
state in which the child[ren] [were] habitually resident immediately before the
removal or retention", there are two principal issues raised on this
application. They are:

1. Has there been a "wrongful retention" of the children
here in issue as contemplated by
Article 3
and as judicially construed? and
2. Assuming an affirmative answer to the first question, has the respondent
satisfied the court her situation falls within any of the exceptions
contemplated by
Article
13?

[
19
]

At the risk of some over-simplification, I think
the positions of the parties may be briefly summarized. Counsel for the father
contends that, upon any intelligent reading of the orders emanating from the
Israeli Court, as well as Sections 14 and 15 of the
Capacity and
Guardianship Law, supra,
it cannot be gainsaid that the applicant/father
enjoyed a right of custody of the minor children. Likewise, it is contended,
upon the undisputed facts, Lidiya and Alis were, in effect, abducted and taken
to Canada, where they were retained; contrary to the express provisions of the
Court's order and contrary to the common understanding and expressed intentions
of the parties. That retention of the children Ms. Zisman submits, is wrongful,
within the meaning of
Article 3.

[
20
]

It is further contended on behalf of the father
that, there is no evidence before the court based on which it could reasonably
find that the mother has established any of the exceptions referred to in
Article
13.
Simply put, the mother's affidavit evidence amounts to no more than
bold allegations, unsupported by any corroborative evidence, not even in those
circumstances where its absence speaks volumes; in other words there is a
deafening silence in respect of all Israeli agencies: government, professional
and non-governmental.

[
21
]

Counsel or the mother contends, among other
things, that the father had a right of access only, which is not the right
protected under the
Convention.
The conclusion, it is argued, flows from
a plain reading of the divorce DECISION. Even if the court is not persuaded by
that argument, Mr. Goldapple submits, the mother's affidavit evidence should be
given full credit. Were the court so to do, the facts of this case falls
clearly within the contemplation of
Article 13,
and, in particular:

(f) There is a grave risk that his or her
return would expose the child to physical or psychological harm or otherwise
place the child in an intolerable situation.

[
22
]

I turn them to a consideration of the first
issue, namely, whether there was a wrongful retention; subservient to which is
the question as to whether the father had a "right of custody".
Article
3
itself sets out the genesis of the rights of custody:

…

The rights of custody mentioned in
subparagraph (a) above, may arise in particular by operation of law or by
reason of a judicial or administrative decision, or by reason of an agreement
having legal effect under the law of that state.

[
23
]

Thomson v. Thomson

(1994),
1994 CanLII 26 (SCC)
, 6 R.F.L.
(4th) 290 (S.C.C.) provides some
guidance as to the meaning of "custody" under
the
Convention:
(at page 316)

Custody, as understood by the Convention,
is a broad term that covers the many situations where a person lawfully has the
care and control of a child. The breach of rights of custody described in art.
3, it will be remembered, are those
attributed
to a person, an
institution, or any other body by the law of the state where the child was
habitually resident immediately before the removal or the retention.

[
24
]

The Court then went on to consider five
situations that may constitute "child abduction" under the
Convention;

the fifth of which it viewed as relevant to the particular circumstances of
that case and, in my view, arguably relevant to the present case:

A …

E. The child was removed from one country
to another in violation of a court order which expressly prohibited such
removal.

The court continued, at page 317:

It by no means follows, however, that the
Convention applies to every case where a child is removed from one country to
another where a court order prohibits it. …the proper view would appear to be
that the mandatory return dictated by the Convention is limited to cases where
the removal is in violation of the custody rights of a person, institution, or
other body. This is the view adopted by Anton [A.E. Anton, "The Hague
Convention on International Child Abduction" (1981) Int. & Comp. L.Q.
53] at pp. 546 and 554-555, who wrote:

It is clear also
from the definitions of custody and access in Article 5 that the removal or
retention of a child in breach merely of access rights would not be wrongful
removal or retention in the sense of Article 3.

…

The convention
contains no mandatory provisions for the support of access rights comparable to
those of its provisions which protect breaches of rights of custody. This
applies even in the extreme case where a child is taken to another country by
the parent with custody rights and is so taken deliberately with a view to
render the further enjoyment of access rights impossible.

[
25
]

The Court, after reviewing some of the
authorities, observed, at page 322, that:

…Under Canadian law, a non-removal clause
may be placed in an interim order of custody to preserve the court's
jurisdiction to make a final determination of custody. It seems to me that when
a court vested with jurisdiction to determine who shall have custody of a
child, it is, while in the course of exercising that jurisdiction, exercising
rights of custody within the broad meaning of the term contemplated by the
Convention. In the words of art.

3(b), "at
the time of the removal or retention those rights were
actually exercised…
or
would have been so exercised but for the removal or retention."

The court went on to find that in the
particular circumstances, "…the Scottish court became 'an institution or
any other body, either jointly or alone, under the law of the State in which
the child was habitually resident immediately before the removal or retention'
having custody rights within the meaning of art. 3". The court continued;
at page 323:

It will be
observed that I have underlined the purely interim nature of the mother's
custody in the present case. I would not wish to be understood as saying the
approach should be the same in a situation where a court inserts a non-removal
clause in a permanent order of custody. Such a clause raises quite different
issues. It is usually intended to ensure permanent access to the non-custodial
parent. The right of access…it was not intended to give it the same level of
protection by the Convention as custody…

[
26
]

Concerning the concept of custody, is one of
mixed fact and law. Accordingly, whether or not rights of custody exist inheres
very much in the particular set of circumstances. Significantly,
Article
5(a)
does not definitively define the term "rights of custody",
and the language of the sub-paragraph necessarily contemplates circumstance,
other than those enumerated, in which rights of custody may arise. In other
words, nomenclature and labels are simply the starting point in any analysis. A
review of the divorce Decision and the contract incorporated into it discloses
no reference to any of the terms "custody", "interim custody"
or "access". What might reasonably be concluded from a reading of the
combined documents, however, is that the children's primary residence would be
with the mother with access to the father. Counsel for both parties predicated
their argument on the claim that each of their clients had custody of the
children in issue. The distinction in their claim is that, in the case of
counsel for the mother, he maintains that the mother's had custody of the two
children in the strictest sense of that term and the father's only rights were
rights of access simpliciter. Counsel for the father maintains, on the other
hand, that it is clear from both the terms of the divorce and from the clear
reading of sections 14 and 15
Israeli Capacity and Guardianship Law.

[
27
]

Although it is open to argument that sections 14
and 15 are subservient to the court's exercise of its jurisdiction relating to
divorce and the custody of children, that argument was not made. Be that as it
may however, it is my view that, read comprehensively, the language of the
divorce decision, including the contract, as it does, as well as the court's
decision in granting leave to remove the child from Israel temporarily makes it
abundantly clear there were residual rights of custody in both the father and
the court itself; in either case, bringing this case clearly within the ambit
of the language of
art. 3.
The language of the decision granting
permission to take the children to Czechoslovakia could not be any clearer.
Paragraph 2 of the Judge Jacob Cohen's decision is to the point:

1. …

2. It is incumbent upon the mother to return the minors to Israel no
later than the date 1.9.04.

[
28
]

The whole tenor of the provisions under the
"children maintenance" caption seem to contemplate and underline the
joint nature of the guardianship of the two children, exemplified in paragraph
(g), where "the partners commit themselves not to take the children
abroad, only on agreement of both partners beforehand and in writing".

[
29
]

The following other circumstances would tend to
reinforce the view of a form of joint guardianship, namely, the required
consent for taking the children abroad; a consent that had to be in writing.
Qualified though the endorsement is, the Court in
Thomson
, supra,
at
page 321 quoting Lord Donaldson M.R. in
C. v. C
.
(Minor: Abduction:
Rights of Custody Abroad)
(1988), [1989] 2 All E.R. 465 (Eng. C.A.), at
473,
recognized the following indicia of rights of custody:

…If anyone, be it an individual or the
court or other institution or a body, has the right to object, and either, is
not consulted or refuses consent, the removal will be wrongful within the
meaning of the convention. I add in the interest of completeness that "a
right to determine the child's place of residence" (using the phrase in the
convention), may be specific, the right to decide that it shall live at a
particular address, or it may be general e.g. "within the Commonwealth of
Australia.

[
30
]

Consistent with the foregoing observation, it is
perfectly reasonable, in my view, given the proper context, to construe the
right of choosing a child's residence as limited to a city, Province or State,
or, at the very most, the country of which the child is a citizen. Such a
construction, does no violence, in my view, to the rights of custody. As I
earlier observed, paragraph (2) of the Decision granting permission to take the
children abroad could not be any more explicit concerning the court's intention
that custody rights should vest in the Israeli courts.

[
31
]

Concluding, therefore, as I have, that there
were custody rights residing in the father and in the institution of the
Israeli court, it remains to be decided whether or not there was a wrongful
retention. It is my view that, on the undisputed facts in this case, once the
mother made the decision to take the children to Canada indefinitely, and acted
on that decision, and continued to act on that decision beyond September 1,
2004, the date on which she was obliged to return the children to Israel, she
had wrongfully retained the children. As noted in
Thomson
, supra,
p.
325, "…a wrongful retention begins from the moment of the expiration of
the period of access, where the original removal was with the consent of [a]
rightful custodian of the child."

[
32
]

It is common ground that the language of
Article
12
is mandatory; in other words, once a wrongful removal or retention has
been established, the requested state is mandated to return the child to the
requesting State unless the abducting parent can bring him/herself within one
of the exceptions contemplated by
Arti
cle 13.

The only two exceptions that were seriously
canvassed were the (a) the claim that "there is a grave risk that [their]
return would expose the child[ren] to physical or psychological harm, or
otherwise place the child[ren] in an intolerable situation, and (b) "the
child objects to being returned and has attained the age and degree of maturity
at which it is appropriate to take account of its views.

[
33
]

Concerning the "…grave risk that…return
would expose the child to physical or psychological harm…" the Court made
the following observation in
Thomson
, supra,
at page 328:

It has been generally accepted that the
Convention mandates a more stringent test than that advanced by the appellant.
In brief, although the word "grave" modifies "risk" and not
"harm", this must be read in conjunction with the clause "or
otherwise

place the child in an intolerable situation". The use of the word
"otherwise" points inescapably to the conclusion that physical or
psychological harm contemplated by the first clause of Art. 13(b) is harm to a
degree that also amounts to an intolerable situation… In
re A (A minor)
(abduction), supra,
[1988] 1 F.L.R. 365 (C.A.) Nourse L.J., in my view
correctly, expressed the approach that should be taken, at p. 372:

…the risk has to
be more than an ordinary risk, or something greater than would normally be
expected on taking a child away from one parent and passing him to another. I
agree…that not only must the risk be a weighty one, but that it must be one of
substantial, and not trivial, psychological harm. That, as it seems to me, is
the effect of the words "or otherwise place the child in an intolerable
situation".

[
34
]

The Court then went on to reject the view that
the only harm contemplated by the
Convention
was that arising from
returning the child, and added; at pp. 328-29:

…from a child-centered perspective, harm is
harm. If the harm were severe enough to meet the stringent test of the
Convention, it would be irrelevant from whence it came. I should observe,
however, that it could only be in the rarest of cases that the effects of
"settling in" to the abductor's environment would constitute a level
of harm contemplated by the Convention. By stating that before one year has
elapsed the rule is that the child must be returned forthwith, art. 12 makes it
clear that the ordinary effects of settling in, therefore, do not warrant
refusal to surrender. Even after the expiration of one year, return must be
ordered unless, in the words of the Convention, "it is demonstrated that
the child is now settled in its new environment".

Put briefly, it is within the contemplation
of the
Convention
that some degree of disequilibrium in the child's life
inheres in the very process of seeking the child's return.

[
35
]

I adverted earlier in these reasons to the
"evidence" adduced on behalf of the mother's assertion of her right
to being excepted pursuant to
art. 13.
As I earlier intimated, the
mother's assertions amount to no more than that; assertions. There is a virtual
dearth of supporting evidence from all the expected sources, in support of the
bald assertions. Counsel for the wife, in part, relied on
Pollastro v.
Pollastro
(1999),
1999 CanLII 3702 (ON CA)
, 45 R.F.L. (4th) 404 (Ont. C.A.). That
case adds little, if anything, to the debate so far as the applicable
principles are concerned, and so egregious were the facts (not mere assertions)
in that case that it is easily understandable why the court concluded as it
did. Accordingly, that decision does not, in my view, advance the mother's
argument.

[
36
]

I turn next to a consideration of Liliya's
putative objection, reproduced at pages 6-7,
supra.
I formed no personal
view as to her maturity but it was not strongly suggested that she lacked the
maturity to assert an objection. Accordingly, for the purposes of these
reasons, she is presumed to possess the necessary maturity. Generously read, it
is probably open to a court to find that Liliya's note/letter constitutes an
objection within the meaning of
Article 13.
Without in any way
denigrating the sentiments expressed by Liliya, the court should be cautious in
assigning undue weight to such a document, given the almost inescapable
conclusion that the sentiments expressed no doubt mirror some of the mother's
sentiments; concerning whose evidence I have earlier commented. Objectively
read the sentiments expressed by Liliya are no more, in my view, than those
often expressed by a child caught in the vortex of a custody battle. That being
the case, it is clear on the authorities that those are issues best dealt with
by the courts in the jurisdiction in which the child was habitually resident
immediately before the removal or the retention. In that regard reference might
usefully be made to
Thome v. Dryden-Hall
(1995),
1995 CanLII 984 (BC SC)
, 18 R.F.L. (4th) 15
(B.C. S.C.) and, as was noted in
Hawke v. Gamble
(1998),
1998 CanLII 3281 (BC SC)
, 43 R.F.L. (4th)
67 (B.C. S.C.) at p. 86:

The best forum to ascertain the wishes of
the children is in a custody trial where experts capable of assessing these
things are called to give evidence tested by cross-examination. Other than
claims by Mr. and Mrs. Gamble, and her mother, there presently is no
independent, reliable evidence before me concerning the wishes of the children.

[
37
]

I note, in passing, that the children in
Hawke
v
.
Gamble
, supra,
were 10 and 7 years of age respectively; and, as
in the present case, the children were not interviewed by the trial judge,
McKinnon J. Concluding, at page 87, that the 10-year old may have been of
sufficient maturity to express a view, the learned judge went on to express his
own fears as to whether he would have the skills necessary to gauge whether any
such expressed views would be truly the child's.

[
38
]

One other issue raised during the course of this
hearing related to what impact, if any, the fact of the mother's claim on
behalf of herself and the two children for refugee status should have on these
proceedings. I shall not dwell on that issue beyond making the observation that
a spirit of urgency infuses the
Convention
and, as is so well canvassed
by Ferrier J. in
Kovacs v
.
Kovacs
(2002),
2002 CanLII 49485 (ON SC)
, 59 O.R. (3d) 671 (Ont.
S.C.J.), lethargy is more characteristic of the process
involving refugee claimants. There is no doubt in my mind that, assuming some
conflict, real or perceived, between the two regimes, the paramountcy must
favour the requested State's obligations under the
Convention.

[
39
]

For all the foregoing reasons, the order sought
will be granted. The applicant shall have his costs of these proceedings,
concerning which, if the parties cannot agree, I am prepared to entertain
written submissions, after they have been exchanged by counsel, within thirty
(30) days of the date of these reasons.

Application granted.
